title: NatWest Boxed’s Andy Ellis on BNPL Rules and Retail Finance
snippet: NatWest Boxed CEO Andy Ellis says the UK's new BNPL rules give retailers the chance to take back ownership of consumer credit at the point of purchase. The post NatWest Boxed’s Andy Ellis on BNPL Rules and Retail Finance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Buy now, pay later came under Financial Conduct Authority regulation in July, when the UK’s rules for deferred payment credit took effect after years of consultation. For the first time, the interest-free instalment plans offered at online checkouts carry affordability checks, standard pre-contract information and access to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

Andy Ellis, CEO at NatWest Boxed

Andy Ellis, chief executive of NatWest Boxed, the embedded finance business owned by NatWest, told The Fintech Times why he thinks the rules matter as much for retailers as for lenders, and what a bank-backed model brings to the market.

Ellis’s argument starts with what retailers gave away when they handed checkout credit to third parties. “What retailers have given up is ownership of an important part of customer relationships,” he said. “When you outsource consumer credit, you aren’t necessarily just outsourcing the lending. In many cases, you are allowing another provider to establish its own relationship with your customer at a really important point in the purchasing journey.”

Those providers, he said, “often go beyond simply facilitating that original transaction for the retailer. They have also developed a monetisation model from building a relationship with the retailer’s customers and marketing other services to them.”

Regulation, in his view, has given retailers a reason to revisit that arrangement. “Retailers have never had a stronger incentive to take ownership of the consumer credit experience,” he said. “This regulation has simply created a natural moment to reassess the previous model.”

The rules themselves centre on affordability and customer outcomes. Ellis described the main concern being addressed as Consumer Duty, the FCA’s requirement that firms deliver good outcomes for customers. Providers must now carry out creditworthiness and affordability assessments, give clearer information before an agreement is signed, and give customers a route to the Financial Ombudsman Service if something goes wrong. “For customers, that should mean greater transparency and stronger, more consistent protections,” he said. “For retailers, it gives them greater confidence and certainty about the standards providers are expected to meet.”

He expects the line between BNPL and other regulated retail finance to blur as a result. “Shoppers will increasingly care less about what a product is called and more about whether it gives them the flexibility, protection and experience they need.”

That shift underpins NatWest Boxed’s own move into the market. The bank-owned embedded finance business already works with UK brands including The AA, Saga and Sainsbury’s, and is adding BNPL to a wider range of lending products. “Retail finance has always been part of our long-term strategy, and the new regulatory framework reinforces the direction the market was already moving in,” Ellis said. “We’re entering a more mature phase where convenience still matters, but so do trust, responsible lending and customer protection.”

He does not present it as a contest between banks and the established BNPL firms. “I think there will continue to be room for different models,” he said. “We were built on regulated banking infrastructure from day one, so regulation isn’t something we’re having to adapt our business model around.”

For retailers, he argues, the opportunity is to treat credit as part of the overall proposition rather than a single button at checkout. “There is no single option that works for every customer at every purchase,” he said. “One customer might want to spread a purchase over a relatively short period, while another purchase might be better suited to a different form of regulated credit.” That, he said, means “offering customers greater choice that keeps the experience embedded within the retailer’s own journey and brand.”

For shoppers, he put the principle simply: “customers should not have to choose between flexibility and protection.” He does not expect flexible payment to go away. “What should change is the confidence customers can have that whichever regulated option they choose, there are appropriate checks, clear information and protections behind it.”

Over the next two years he expects the distinctions between deferred payment credit and other regulated retail finance to become less pronounced from the customer’s point of view, and retailers to think less about product categories and more about outcomes. “It’s not necessarily as simple as winners and losers because different business models will continue to coexist,” he said. “However, the providers that can combine a strong customer experience with trust and responsible lending will emerge as the clear leaders in the market.”

title: Wise Adds eSIM Plans and Cross-continent QR Payments to Travel Hub
snippet: Wise has expanded its Travel Hub with customisable eSIM data plans and a unified QR payment scanner covering local schemes across five continents. The post Wise Adds eSIM Plans and Cross-continent QR Payments to Travel Hub appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Wise has expanded its in-app Travel Hub with two new features aimed at international travellers: customisable eSIM data plans and a unified QR code payment scanner that connects to local payment schemes across five continents. Both features are live from 6 October 2026 for Wise Account holders in the UK, the European Economic Area, the US, Canada, Brazil, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia and New Zealand.

The eSIM offering, powered by infrastructure provider Gigs U.K. Ltd, gives travellers the ability to set their own data allowance and coverage duration rather than buying pre-packaged roaming bundles. Wise says it will refund unused data plans, a feature it is positioning as a differentiator in a telco market where surplus data is typically forfeited. Standard regional plans cover more than 150 destinations. The one-time installation model means the eSIM does not need to be re-downloaded for each trip.

Connecting to domestic QR networks

The QR payment integration is arguably the more structurally interesting development. Wise has built direct connections to a range of domestic real-time payment schemes that have historically been inaccessible to foreign visitors: PayNow in Singapore, DuitNow in Malaysia, Pix in Brazil, PromptPay in Thailand, QR Ph in the Philippines, Swiss QR-bill and Qvik in Hungary. A partnership with Alipay+, Ant International‘s multi-wallet gateway, extends the reach to millions of merchants on the Chinese mainland, where foreign cards and cash are rarely accepted, as well as across 50 destinations including Hong Kong, South Korea and Cambodia.

A Wise spokesperson described the problem the product addresses: “Your phone has no signal, you can’t look up directions, and you realise the local taxi or coffee shop doesn’t accept your card. It instantly makes you feel isolated and locked out of the local economy.”

A Wise-commissioned YouGov survey of more than 14,000 travellers across eleven countries found that 62% of international travellers rely on hotel Wi-Fi to stay connected abroad, and that 43% cited cash management as their most common payment problem overseas. Around 40% said connectivity limitations had caused them to skip local experiences such as street food markets.

Market context and competitive read-across

Wise’s move reflects a broader push by cross-border payment platforms to extend their value proposition beyond currency conversion. Revolut, a close competitor, has offered eSIM connectivity through its app for some time, making it a direct point of comparison. Monzo and other neobanks have expanded travel-related features but have not yet replicated the domestic QR network integration at this geographic scale.

The QR integration is particularly relevant from a payments infrastructure perspective. Domestic instant payment schemes built on QR standards, such as Pix, PayNow and PromptPay, have grown rapidly and now represent primary payment rails in several markets rather than supplementary options. For cross-border players, gaining access to these rails through direct scheme connections or gateway partnerships is increasingly a competitive necessity rather than a differentiator. Wise’s partnership with Alipay+ is notable because it provides access to the Chinese market without requiring a local banking relationship, a barrier that has limited most Western fintechs.

Wise reported processing over $240 billion in cross-border transactions in the financial year 2026, serving around 19 million customers. The Travel Hub expansion sits alongside pay-as-you-go airport lounge passes, multi-currency group bill splitting and in-app country guides, all of which position the Wise Account as a broader travel wallet rather than a pure foreign exchange tool. Whether that bundling strategy drives account activation or deepens engagement among existing customers is the commercial question the company has not yet answered with disclosed data.

title: Money20/20 USA Unveils 2026 Agenda Focused on AI Transformation, Borderless Infrastructure, and Regulatory Guardrails
snippet: Money20/20 USA 2026 in Las Vegas will explore borderless payments, AI transformation, strategic partnerships and regulation, bringing together leaders shaping the future of financial services. The post Money20/20 USA Unveils 2026 Agenda Focused on AI Transformation, Borderless Infrastructure, and Regulatory Guardrails appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
As global financial markets confront rapid technological convergence, evolving regulatory expectations, and the rise of autonomous agentic commerce, Money20/20 USA has officially unveiled the agenda for its 2026 conference. Convening at The Venetian in Las Vegas from October 18–21, the world’s flagship fintech gathering will bring together thousands of industry leaders, central bankers, institutional investors, and startup founders.

The 2026 event features an expanded architectural footprint spanning eight specialized stages: the Exchange Stage, the Intersection Stage, the Mastertrack & Deep Dive Stage, the Arra.i.val Stage, the MoneyPot Stage, the Partner Stage, the Startup Hub Stage, and the RiseUp & Amplify Stage. Incorporating more sponsors and exhibitors than previous editions—including over 180 institutions making their event debut—the gathering serves as a global venue for dealmaking, platform launches, and strategic partnership formation.

Four Core Pillars Reshaping Global Financial Infrastructure

The 2026 agenda is structured around four primary thematic pillars designed to address structural shifts in global money movement:

Borderless Financial Architecture: Examining cross-border clearing, multi-currency liquidity rails, and interoperable payment networks.

Technology as the Great Equalizer: Analyzing artificial intelligence, machine learning, and automated software infrastructure driving operational speed and financial access.

Partnerships as the Engine to Scale: Highlighting collaborative execution models between incumbent banking institutions, fintech scaleups, and big tech providers.

Brave New World — Setting Guardrails: Evaluating regulatory compliance, risk management models, and systemic safety mechanisms required to govern digital assets and automated money.

A central highlight of this year’s agenda is the expanded “The Intersection” activation area, bringing together leaders sitting at the nexus of geopolitical shifts, market volatility, and systemic risk. Speakers include former CFTC Chairman J. Christopher Giancarlo, Fireblocks CEO Michael Shaulov, and Karin Kusano.

The track also features the World Gold Council introducing its “Gold as a Service” initiative, establishing a standardized market infrastructure to connect physical gold custody directly with digital asset applications and tokenized financial products.

“Gold is evolving to unlock its full potential in the digital economy,” stated David Tait, CEO of the World Gold Council. “At Money20/20 USA, we are thrilled to bring Gold as a Service to the fintech community. This initiative bridges physical gold with the digital world, increasing access and improving tradability of the world’s most resilient asset.”

Keynote Lineup and Institutional Innovation

The 2026 speaker lineup brings together traditional banking leaders, global market utilities, and venture capital investors. Keynote presenters include William (Bill) Demchak, Chairman & CEO of The PNC Financial Services Group; Racquel Oden, US Head of International Wealth & Global Private Banking at HSBC; Cameron Fowler, CEO of Early Warning; and Leigh Amaro, CEO Americas at SWIFT.

They are joined by enterprise decision-makers and venture partners, including Andrew Reed (Sequoia Capital), David Jegen (F-Prime), Tarek Mansour (Kalshi), Brandon Millman (Phantom), Mariëtte Swart (Adyen), Dipti Kachru (State Street), Ana Carla Abrão (Open Finance Brazil), and Marie-Elise Droga (EBANX).

Simultaneously, the Startup Hub Stage will spotlight founders building next-generation compliance tools, real-world asset (RWA) tokenization platforms, and embedded financial infrastructure. Key sessions will address regional expansion strategies, venture capital trends in the AI era, and institutional adoption across stablecoins and tokenized yield.

“The future of finance is being built right now, and Money20/20 is where the people building it come together,” noted Jessica Blue, executive vice president of Money20/20 USA. “Our 2026 experience will offer new formats combining networking with content and will include more debates and deep dive interactive sessions, where participants will turn insight into action.”

As financial infrastructure pivots toward continuous, borderless, and intelligent settlement, Money20/20 USA 2026 provides the key forum defining the commercial roadmap for modern financial services.

title: Etraveli Group Rebrands Precision as Standalone Travel Fintech Arm
snippet: The Stockholm flight-tech group is repositioning Precision from a risk tool into a dedicated fintech business serving airlines and OTAs. The post Etraveli Group Rebrands Precision as Standalone Travel Fintech Arm appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Etraveli Group has formally rebranded Precision, previously known primarily as an internal risk management solution, as the group’s dedicated travel fintech division. The repositioning, announced on 6 October 2026, broadens Precision’s scope beyond fraud controls and gives it a commercial identity as a standalone B2B fintech provider serving airlines, online travel agencies and global travel businesses.

Peny Rizou, chief fintech officer of Etraveli Group and head of Precision

The refreshed Precision launches with two named products. Precision Fraud Prevention uses machine learning models trained on travel-specific transaction data to help clients approve a higher proportion of legitimate bookings while containing fraud losses. Precision Travel Flexibility is a decisioning layer that allows travel companies to offer contextual cancellation and change options, adjusting eligibility and pricing at the individual booking level to lift attachment rates and protect margin. Etraveli says both products are designed around the structural realities of the travel sector, notably thin margins, high cancellation volumes and significant exposure to card-not-present fraud.

Peny Rizou, chief fintech officer of Etraveli Group and head of Precision, framed the move as an external commercialisation of capabilities developed over two decades of internal use. “Over two decades, we have honed these capabilities internally. By evolving Precision into a specialised fintech arm, we are giving airlines, OTAs and travel partners access to travel-native intelligence that turns challenges like fraud and cancellation risks into scalable, profit-generating strategies.”

Precision already has named distribution relationships with Outpayce by Amadeus, Mastercard Gateway, Sabre and Checkout.com, which collectively represent substantial coverage of the global flight booking and payments infrastructure. Etraveli did not disclose revenue attributable to Precision, nor the split between internal group usage and third-party client contracts.

Market context

The travel payments and fraud-prevention segment has attracted growing fintech interest as airlines and OTAs look to recover margin lost to high chargeback rates and the operational cost of flexible ticketing rules introduced widely during the pandemic period. Several specialist vendors, including Forter, Signifyd and Riskified, already compete in the transaction-level fraud decisioning space across verticals. Precision’s stated differentiation is domain specificity: models trained solely on travel data rather than cross-vertical datasets, which the company argues improves approval accuracy for the irregular purchase patterns typical of flight bookings.

The Travel Flexibility product places Etraveli in a narrower but expanding category. With regulators in the EU and UK maintaining or tightening consumer rights around flight disruption, airlines face commercial pressure to package flexibility as an upsell rather than absorb it as a liability. A decisioning layer that prices and distributes those options dynamically carries revenue-share potential that fraud tooling alone does not.

Competitive positioning

Etraveli’s structural advantage is captive transaction volume. The group processes flight bookings for Booking.com, Google Flights, Skyscanner and Kayak, and operates its own consumer OTA brands including Gotogate and Mytrip. That proprietary data estate underpins the machine learning claims in a way a pure-play vendor without comparable volume cannot easily replicate. However, the durability of that advantage depends on whether Precision can demonstrate model lift over general-purpose fraud tools to external clients who already have incumbent vendor relationships.

Etraveli is backed by CVC Capital Partners and KKR. It employs more than 3,200 people across 11 offices and serves over 48 million travellers annually in more than 75 markets. The group did not indicate whether Precision is being positioned for a separate capital raise or eventual spin-out, nor whether the repositioning is accompanied by any change in headcount or cost structure within the division.

title: Lumepay’s Luc Varejes on fixing the plumbing of African cross-border payments, starting in Kenya
snippet: Lumepay Obtains Regulatory Clearance to Launch Multi-Rail Cross-Border Payment Infrastructure in Kenya The post Lumepay’s Luc Varejes on fixing the plumbing of African cross-border payments, starting in Kenya appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Lumepay, the Cape Town-based cross-border payments company built for SMEs, corporates and institutions that need to move money across Africa and into global markets, is launching in Kenya this month, the first market on its African expansion roadmap. It arrives with regulatory clearance in hand, in the form of a letter of no objection, and a licensed local partner, and it will be on the ground at the Africa Blockchain Fest in Nairobi from 15 to 17 October.

Luc Varejes, chief operating officer at Lumepay

Its chief operating officer, Luc Varejes, spoke to The Fintech Times about the structural problem Lumepay is built to solve, why Kenya is a hub rather than a single-market play, what the launch means in practice for Kenyan businesses, and where the company wants to be in five years.

Fixing the plumbing

For Varejes, the gap Lumepay is closing is not a product gap but a structural one. “For decades, moving value across African borders has meant going through a fragmented web of correspondent banks, multiple intermediaries and layered currency conversions. Each step adds cost, delay and uncertainty,” he said. By Lumepay’s estimate the result is a system that costs African businesses around five billion dollars a year in inefficiencies, “and for a business, that shows up as tied-up working capital, unpredictable settlement times and pricing that is hard to plan around.”

The company’s answer is to work on the infrastructure itself rather than the interface on top of it. “Our focus is on fixing the plumbing,” Varejes said. “We are building regional payment corridors and deep liquidity pools across the SADC and WAEMU regions, which strengthens Africa’s financial connectivity both within the continent and with the rest of the world.” Operationally that means combining “the reach and reliability of traditional payment infrastructure with the speed and efficiency of stablecoin rails”, which he said gives businesses “faster settlement, more competitive and predictable pricing, and the confidence that their payments will arrive when they need them to.”

Why Kenya, and why now

Varejes gave three reasons for choosing Kenya as the first stop. The first is trade. “The South Africa-Kenya corridor is a fastest-growing trade route. South African and Kenyan businesses are trading with each other more than ever, but the payment infrastructure hasn’t kept pace,” he said. “Settling a supplier invoice between Johannesburg and Nairobi still too often means going through correspondent banks in another currency, with the delays and costs that come with it.”

The second is geography. Kenya has one of the most mature digital payments ecosystems in the world, driven largely by mobile money, and strong regional links into Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and beyond. “For us, Kenya isn’t a single-market play,” Varejes said. “It’s the hub that connects our southern and western corridors to the broader East African Community.”

The third is that the volumes already exist. He pointed to the 2025 remittances household survey by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics and the Central Bank of Kenya, which found that Kenyan households received an estimated KSh931.8 billion from abroad between June 2024 and May 2025, while residents sent KSh40.5 billion out of the country over the same period. “And that’s only the household side,” he said. “Money crosses Kenya’s borders every day to finance trade, pay suppliers and fund investment. The demand for faster, more cost-effective cross-border payments is clear.”

As for the timing: “The market is ready, and so are we. With regulatory clearance in place and a licensed local partner, we can enter Kenya with the right foundations to serve businesses from day one.”

What the launch means in practice

Asked what Kenyan businesses will actually be able to do from launch, Varejes described a set of concrete use cases. A business can pay international suppliers in the supplier’s own currency, such as US dollars or Chinese yuan, so an SME settling offshore invoices “can settle in each supplier’s preferred currency faster, and without costly conversions. Suppliers get paid in their expected currency.”

Businesses operating in Kenya can also access US dollars instantly. “No more funds stuck in transit for months,” he said. “Businesses can confidently grow across Africa, with the certainty that money moves.” A merchant making bulk payments can pay “quickly and compliantly across many recipients and currencies at once, settling hundreds of payouts in a single flow.” Alongside that sit diversified ways to send and receive local and other currencies, including USDT on-ramps and off-ramps and M-Pesa, and payment links.

Further information about the company’s cross-border payment services is available on Lumepay.com.

Where Lumepay sits

The distinction Varejes draws from the rest of the market starts with the rails. “We use our own stablecoin infrastructure, built and supported by us, to make every payment more efficient,” he said. Lumepay’s own account of its position is that its advantage lies in developing strong traditional, digital (stablecoin-enabled) and FX capabilities that together compound in value: operating depth across traditional banking rails, stablecoins and FX, where the market tends to offer one or two of the three, and “going to market with all three, from the get-go, with deep African context.”

He is candid that the hardest part is not technology but liquidity. “Africa has its unique challenges: FX liquidity limitations at financial institutions, settlements that take weeks, laborious compliance processes. Deep liquidity that moves and routes with efficiency is key to moving value, and takes years to build up. We’ve already built it and are actively growing and optimising our liquidity.” Every founder, he added, has personally set up, scaled or led functions inside cross-border payments businesses. “We are accelerating, not researching.”

In Varejes’s description, Lumepay sits across the full transaction lifecycle. “Currency exchange, liquidity management, clearing, payments collections and disbursements, and settlement infrastructure, all within a single licensed perimeter. Customers operate through one integrated platform rather than coordinating across multiple vendors and intermediaries.” The role, he said, extends beyond being a conversion or pay-out venue: “Lumepay is the end-to-end cross-border solutions and infrastructure layer that supports execution, post-trade processing, reconciliation, and settlement across multiple rails and jurisdictions.”

That is also how he frames the company’s relationship with the incumbents. “The ecosystem we are building is not about replacing every existing provider, it is about creating the connective infrastructure that lets the broader financial system operate seamlessly, efficiently, and transparently across borders.”

Lumepay’s competitive advantage

According to Lumepay, its competitive position rests on combining traditional banking infrastructure, stablecoin-enabled payment rails and foreign exchange capabilities, alongside experience operating in African markets.

Business model and infrastructure. Lumepay says its team has experience across traditional banking, stablecoins and FX. Its strategy is to bring these capabilities together in a single offering, rather than relying on one or two components.

Africa-specific understanding. The company identifies limited FX liquidity, lengthy settlement processes and demanding compliance requirements as challenges in African cross-border payments. It says developing deep, efficiently routed liquidity is central to addressing them.

Execution and speed to market. Lumepay says its founders have established, scaled or led cross-border payments functions, bringing operational experience and existing capabilities to the business.

Stablecoin-enabled settlement. The company views stablecoins as a tool for moving value and expects broader adoption as regulation and access develop. It argues that liquidity, licences and connections to traditional banking remain important to scaling these services.

The next five years

Kenya is the first market on the roadmap, and Varejes set out the five outcomes Lumepay is building towards over the next five years: a diversified customer base across markets and sectors, with reach and regular payments activity across key African markets; reliable and regulated multi-corridor payment infrastructure, liquidity and market coverage; the strongest wholesale pricing and deepest liquidity across all African currency pairs; key licences across all major African markets; and a robust, high-speed stablecoin settlement layer.

Stablecoin adoption, he argued, strengthens rather than threatens that position. “As it becomes more regulated and accessible, more players will naturally try capture the opportunity, but we will be at the forefront of the ecosystem and capabilities built around it to successfully scale: deep, diversified liquidity across corridors; the licensing to operate legally in each market; and the bridge between stablecoin and traditional banking that moves value reliably.”

On the ground in Nairobi

Lumepay will be at the Africa Blockchain Fest from 15 to 17 October, and Varejes sees the event as the right place to start. “It brings together the people building the next phase of African finance and trade. We strongly believe in being on the ground so we can hear directly from the people we aim to serve.”

The message he wants people to leave with is a simple one. “Lumepay’s focus is helping African businesses grow beyond their home markets without payment friction getting in the way.”

For more information, visit Lumepay.com.

title: Airtel Money Prices LSE Listing at $7bn on Institutional Demand
snippet: Airtel Africa's mobile money arm raised $700m in a London secondary offering backed by the IFC, TPG, Mastercard and Qatar's sovereign wealth fund. The post Airtel Money Prices LSE Listing at $7bn on Institutional Demand appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Airtel Money has completed pricing for its London Stock Exchange listing at a $7 billion valuation, equivalent to $2.60 per share, as Airtel Africa and a group of existing shareholders offloaded a 270 million share block to generate roughly $700 million in proceeds.

The transaction is a secondary offering rather than a primary capital raise. No new equity was issued into the operational balance sheet; existing investors are using the listing to crystallise returns and establish a public market reference price for the mobile money subsidiary. Airtel Africa retains the asset on its books at a formally audited market value, which matters for how the parent company’s equity is priced by institutional investors.

The institutional architecture of the deal

The cornerstone order came from the International Finance Corporation, the private sector lending arm of the World Bank, which committed $90 million to purchase shares at the final offer price. That commitment is structured as a secondary buyout, absorbing equity sold down by existing holders rather than providing fresh growth capital. Multilateral anchoring of this kind is a standard backstop mechanism for emerging-market listings, and the IFC’s participation signals that the asset meets development-finance screening criteria, which in turn reassures commercial institutions on governance and anti-money-laundering standards.

Alongside the IFC, the syndicate includes existing minority shareholders TPG‘s The Rise Fund, Mastercard, Qatar Investment Authority, and Chimetech, which collectively injected $550 million into the business in 2021. Each is now using the listing to partially reduce exposure. Full unconditional settlement on the LSE main market is scheduled for mid-October, with conditional trading already under way.

The deal was co-managed by Citigroup, Barclays, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan Chase. The tight 16.5 per cent free float was calibrated for sovereign wealth vehicles, emerging-market hedge funds, and global asset managers seeking direct equity exposure to African mobile payment infrastructure without taking on the consolidated telecom balance sheet.

The $7 billion final valuation represents a material discount to the $8 billion-plus figures that were being discussed earlier in 2026, reflecting persistent compression in UK public market multiples for technology assets. London’s IPO market has struggled to attract and retain high-growth technology listings, a structural concern the FCA and HM Treasury have been addressing through the Edinburgh Reforms and subsequent changes to the UK Listing Rules that came into effect in 2024.

Fundamentals and market context

The underlying platform processes more than $200 billion in total transaction value annually across 13 African markets, generating approximately $1.3 billion in revenue with an EBITDA margin of close to 50 per cent. Those unit economics put Airtel Money in a category alongside M-Pesa and Wave as one of the few mobile money operators on the continent with both scale and demonstrable profitability.

The listing arrives as African mobile money infrastructure attracts growing institutional attention. The IFC’s involvement, and the participation of a major card network in Mastercard, underlines that the sector is no longer viewed purely through a development-finance lens but as a commercially investable payment rail with defensible network effects. For the broader African fintech ecosystem, the deal provides a public comparable valuation that other operators and their investors will reference in future fundraising rounds and M&A negotiations.

The near-term question is whether the listing improves Airtel Money’s regulatory positioning across its 13 markets. A publicly listed entity with multilateral shareholders and a formal LSE disclosure regime carries a different compliance profile than a privately held telecom subsidiary, which may smooth licensing conversations with central banks in markets where mobile money regulation is still maturing.

title: How agentic payments present risk
snippet: “There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate,” writes one financial services consultant. “That's a problem for issuers as they contemplate making credentials available to AI tools.”
fullText:
Aaron Cheiffetz is an analyst and executive strategist in the financial services industry, working with banking leaders on artificial intelligence governance, enterprise architecture, regulatory compliance and operational resiliency. He is based in Charlotte, North Carolina.

In the debit-card context, Regulation E generally limits a consumer's liability for unauthorized transfers involving a lost or stolen debit card to $50 if the loss is reported within two business days. But Regulation E excludes from its definition of an “unauthorized electronic fund transfer” a transfer initiated by a person to whom the consumer furnished the access device, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that transfers by that person are no longer authorized. 

The official commentary goes further: if a consumer furnishes an access device and grants another person authority to make transfers, the consumer can remain liable even when that person exceeds the authority given. Regulation E defines "person" to include both natural persons and organizations, including corporations. 

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Aaron Cheiffetz

What it doesn't say is how that rule applies when credentials are furnished to software operated by a company. A January research report by the Consumer Bankers Association asks whether sharing credentials with an AI tool could trigger this exclusion and leave the consumer responsible for the agent's mistakes.

In the credit-card context, the Truth in Lending Act, implemented by Regulation Z, provides a similar unauthorized-use framework that turns on whether another person had actual, implied, or apparent authority to use the account. Here too, it's unclear how that rule applies when an AI tool acts on a cardholder's behalf.

Visa and Mastercard have zero-liability policies for unauthorized transactions that go beyond federal law. But those policies still depend on a transaction being classified as unauthorized. They don't clearly resolve what happens when a consumer authorized an agent to transact but disputes whether a particular purchase fell within the scope of that authority. 

These are the kinds of issues that should be addressed in agentic payment frameworks, which Mastercard and Visa are developing. Such frameworks envision the payment system recording or validating instructions given by users to agents and taking steps to make sure agents and merchants are who they purport to be and that transactions remain consistent with the consumer's mandate. 

But a host of questions remain. There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate. That's a problem for issuers as they contemplate making credentials available to AI tools. 

Where risks aren't adequately addressed and priced, issuers may be tempted to act defensively by agreeing to credential-sharing only with sophisticated AI-tool providers under negotiated contracts, adopting onerous identity-confirmation processes, or refusing transactions in some circumstances. All of this would tilt the playing field in favor of incumbent platforms.

Some clarity about liability for unauthorized transactions will be important before agentic payments are rolled out more broadly. Voluntary efforts by banks and payment networks won't go far enough to assuage concerns. More fundamental issues of consumer liability need to be addressed. 

At minimum, three things need to happen. 

First, laws should distinguish between a consumer’s own acts and the acts of others, including AI tools acting on a consumer's behalf. Second, when consumers give others authority to initiate financial transactions, the parameters of that authority, such as amounts, merchants, timing, and other limits, should be documented in a form the payment system can use. Third, the allocation of losses among issuers, payment networks, merchants, and AI-tool providers should not be an issue for consumers.

Firms crack down on money mules but need to do more

              

  

  

  
    

    

      

Financial firms are shutting down hundreds of thousands of suspected money mule accounts, but organised criminal groups are still shifting dirty money through multiple bank accounts before cashing out.

  

            						

An FCA survey found firms have closed an increasing number of suspected mule accounts over the last 3 years: 238,396 suspected mules had their accounts closed in 2025, up from 184,935 in 2023 and 233,269 in 2024.

An increase in account closures could reflect broader customer growth alongside improvements in identifying and acting on suspected mule activity, rather than necessarily meaning mules make up a higher proportion of firms’ business.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates more than £100bn is laundered through the UK or UK corporate structures each year. Money mule activity is one way criminals move these funds, by using people’s bank accounts to receive or transfer money on their behalf.

Account closures were highest among customers aged 26 to 39 (91,073), while the sharpest increase was among customers aged 40 to 49 (37,274 in 2025 up from 25,760 in 2024). Customers aged 25 and under (85,425) also represented a significant proportion of closures.

The financial regulator also found evidence that criminals moved fraudulent funds through multiple accounts, usually cashing out between the second and fifth account. By this stage, payments are harder to detect and trace, and shows that firms need to crack down on activity as early as possible.

Some accounts had been used repeatedly for mule activity before firms shut them down and had also been used for fraud. This points to an established criminal infrastructure rather than opportunistic, isolated incidents.

The FCA, NCA, Home Office, the Treasury and industry are leading on 9 system priorities (PDF) as part of the UK’s response to economic crime. The FCA is playing a key role on the money mules priority by working with industry on an action plan to tackle the problem, including better ways for firms and law enforcement to share intelligence on suspected money mule activity.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Money muling is a crime and it's not victimless. It makes it harder to recover stolen cash and helps criminals move and hide the proceeds of serious offending. People should be wary of contact out of the blue, including via online channels, asking them to funnel money through their account as they could face prosecution.

'It's good that financial firms are taking action on mules, but banks, law enforcement, technology companies and consumers all have a role to play in stopping people being drawn into criminal activity.'

  

Money mule warning signs to look out for

If you’re approached out of the blue online with an offer of quick cash, then alarm bells should ring.  

Scammers may call it a 'job offer' but no legitimate company will ask you to use your own bank account to transfer their money.  

Never give sensitive financial details to someone you don’t know and trust.

Be aware that the consequences of becoming a money mule could include losing access to your bank account and possible prosecution. 

Find out more about money transfer scams.

Notes to editors

Read our multi-firm review: Money mules: mule activity and cashing out findings.

Alongside the National Economic Crime Centre, the FCA is alerting firms to its latest findings.

Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA’s strategic priorities (PDF).

The FCA surveyed 35 retail banks, building societies, challenger banks, payment institutions and e-money institutions.  

The FCA also established a public/private cell in 2025 – a working group with 22 regulated firms. The cell looked at 140 cases, covering 7 types of fraud.

The FCA found card payments were the most common cash-out method and used to make lots of low-value transactions, or higher-value payments to local businesses and retailers. This can resemble legitimate consumer spending and be harder for firms to detect.    

Retail banks accounted for most transactions passing through mule accounts, whereas other firms experience lower volumes but higher-value transactions. This suggests different criminal behaviours, cash-out strategies and risk concentrations. 

The Home Office’s Fraud Strategy 2026 to 2029 recognises the role that money mule networks play in facilitating fraud and financial crime.

This work follows previous publications on detecting and preventing money mules, and firms' use of the National Fraud Database (NFD) and money mule detection tools.

title: Stablecoin startups advance payments
snippet: Entrepreneurs embracing the digital assets are pushing payments modernization forward, and bringing incumbents along too.
fullText:
Fintech entrepreneurs are using stablecoins as a means of breaking into the payments industry and driving digital modernization.

Startups such as MassPay and Rain have been forging new pathways for payments that embrace stablecoins, either incorporating or bypassing aging rails. They see an expansive opportunity ahead as they begin to make inroads.

While traditional payments players, including card network giant Visa and mega processor Fiserv, have also glommed on to the stablecoin trend, their legacy infrastructures may increase the difficulty of adapting to digital schemes.

Meanwhile, younger companies are amassing capital from venture investors and hiring employees to build stablecoin networks and accessories. The appeal for investors has been a simple one, according to Verda Ventures General Partner Alex Witt.

“The basic premise behind our fund is: sending payments should be as easy, fast, and cheap as sending a text message,” Witt said in an interview this month. “We fundamentally believe with blockchain, mobile phones, and the internet, that is completely possible.”

Witt and his business partner, Amit Chu, created a venture fund two years ago to invest in stablecoin startups and it has since drawn $40 million, he said, allowing the fund to purchase minority stakes in about two dozen companies globally. 

It’s a real change from when Witt first started to raise money for the fund in 2024 and people thought he was “completely crazy,” he said.

The Verda portfolio includes the fintech Yellow Card focused on payments in Africa as well as the blockchain infrastructure services company Capa, which operates in Latin America.

Two other companies the fund invested in have already been sold, specifically Kulipa and Beam. In addition, digital processor Stripe is circling another possible purchase, Witt said, declining to name it.

Rain evolves into stablecoin services

Rain’s holding company, Signify, began as a different business and then morphed into the one branded as Rain today. It has collected about $338 million in equity investments along the way, according to a spokesperson for the company. 

Among the private company’s investors are San Francisco investment firm Iconiq Capital, Sapphire Ventures and Coinbase’s former chief technology officer, Balaji Srinivasan, with a quarter of a billion dollars raised in the most recent round disclosed in January.

Rain provides stablecoin infrastructure services that enable corporate customers to bridge stablecoin payments so that money can move from the digital assets to traditional payment rails. Corporate clients embed the technology in their services for consumer use, letting consumers tap stablecoins in a way that’s less invisible to users. 

Early clients were crypto firms, fintechs and neobanks, sometimes in countries where the digital assets acted as a hedge against inflation, such as in Argentina. But then Rain began attracting bigger names, landing remittance provider Western Union as its first major customer last year, then a large peer, MoneyGram, and ticketing company Live Nation followed this year.

This week, Rain said it’s making a digital wallet available to consumers that will enable them to save, spend and send from a stablecoin balance that is backed by cards the company issues. For now, consumers will still custody their funds with the non-custodial wallets, but the company plans to offer custodial wallets by yearend.

Rain expands following Genius Act

Rain has grown by acquisition too. In August, Rain purchased the California payments and technology firm Ansa for an undisclosed sum. 

Now, the business employs about 150 people around the world, with a pack of them located in the New York headquarters, the company’s CEO, Farooq Malik, said in an interview last month.

The brand name Rain dawned on the founders because they saw how fast and fluid funds could be transferred using stablecoins. The same could be said for how quickly startup businesses are reacting to stablecoin developments, like the signing of the Genius Act, which created a regulatory framework for the digital assets.

President Donald Trump’s signing of that new law last year was pivotal in pushing the business forward, Malik said.

“The tipping point was really the Genius Act,” he said. “A lot of people had been waiting on the sidelines for clarity before proceeding. That gave companies and people the confidence to proceed. Consumers also have to believe this is viable.”

Now, the company aims to take another step in its evolution. It applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust charter this month, seeking the ability to offer asset custody and other related services, though they could still accept deposits or make loans. 

MassPay embraces stablecoins

Another startup growing in the stablecoin arena is Las Vegas-based MassPay, which is using the digital asset technology to streamline payments for gig workers, contractors and marketplace sellers as well as providing payout services for gaming and sports betting. It connects to local payment rails, real-time payment systems and mobile wallets.

“We've seen growing demand for stablecoins, primarily by large-scale institutions that feel comfortable due to some clearance in the regulation,” the company’s CEO, Ran Grushkowsky, said in an interview last month. Stablecoins are becoming particularly useful for speed and payments over the weekends, he explained.

The majority of MassPay’s 300 corporate clients are in North America, Grushkowsky said. They include Los Angeles-based online social platform Passes and New York-based marketplace Whop.

Last week, MassPay said it had forged a new integration with Block’s Cash App digital wallet.

MassPay’s services are offered in some 230 countries, according to the press release last December that named Grushkowsky CEO as of this year. The company has grown to process tens of billions of dollars annually, with about half of those payments moving across borders, and about 10% in stablecoins, he said.

The company is privately funded, and now employs about 54 workers, mainly in the U.S., Grushkowsky said. He declined to say how much money the owners have raised. 

As startups nudge stablecoins forward, the digital currency is slowly becoming a real possibility for payments in everyday life, Witt explained. 

“The biggest challenge, though, is that last mile of friction and localizing to consumer preferences,” Witt said. “We wanted to invest in the leaders around the world that are bridging the gap.”

title: ADIB Shareholders Approve AED 1.75bn Rights Issue for Growth Push
snippet: Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank will issue 106 million new shares at AED 16.45 each, raising capital to fund digital expansion and AI investment under The post ADIB Shareholders Approve AED 1.75bn Rights Issue for Growth Push appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank (ADIB) has secured shareholder approval for a rights issue expected to raise approximately AED 1.75 billion in gross proceeds, one of the larger capital raises from a Gulf Islamic lender in recent years. The resolution passed at a General Assembly Meeting on 6 October 2026 by the requisite majority.

The issue comprises 106,383,000 new shares priced at AED 16.45 each, made up of a nominal value of AED 1 and a share premium of AED 15.45. Eligible shareholders will be entitled to subscribe for roughly one new share for every 34.14 shares held. The issue price represents a discount of approximately 28.8% to ADIB’s closing share price on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange on 24 August 2026. On completion, ADIB’s issued and paid-up share capital will rise from AED 3.632 billion to AED 3.738 billion.

Group chief executive Mohamed Abdelbary said the bank had surpassed AED 300 billion in total assets and saw meaningful scope to expand core businesses, deepen customer relationships, and accelerate its digital and AI capabilities. “The additional equity will provide greater capacity to fund this growth while maintaining capital strength,” he said. “Our focus is on deploying that capital with discipline to deliver sustainable returns for shareholders.”

Capital position and recent performance

ADIB’s headline metrics underpin the logic of the raise. Total assets reached AED 304 billion at the end of the first half of 2026, after 24% asset growth across the whole of 2025. Return on equity held at 28% in 2024, rose to 29% in 2025, and remained at 28% through the first half of 2026. Those figures are notably high by global banking standards and suggest the bank is seeking fresh equity not because profitability is under pressure, but because it wants additional headroom to grow its risk-weighted asset base without compressing its capital ratios.

Chairman Jawaan Awaidah Al Khaili said the shareholder vote reflected confidence in the bank’s franchise and its ability to deliver sustainable growth. ADIB intends to publish a prospectus shortly, which will set out the subscription timetable, including the record date, rights trading period and subscription window, subject to regulatory and supervisory approval.

Market and regulatory context

The raise sits within a broader pattern of Gulf bank recapitalisations as institutions in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar look to fund asset-growth ambitions that have outpaced organic capital generation. Islamic banks face the same Basel III capital adequacy requirements as conventional lenders, with the added complexity of structuring instruments that comply with Sharia principles, which rules out standard subordinated debt and additional tier-one structures used by conventional peers. Rights issues remain the most straightforward path to common equity tier-one capital for Islamic lenders.

From a regulatory standpoint, the UAE Central Bank has been raising minimum capital adequacy expectations in line with the final Basel III implementation timeline. A pre-emptive equity raise, undertaken from a position of high profitability, is preferable to a reactive one and gives ADIB flexibility to bid on larger corporate financing mandates and deepen its retail and private banking books.

The proceeds are earmarked in broad terms rather than against a named acquisition or specific product line, which leaves the deployment thesis somewhat open. Investors will be looking at whether the capital accelerates the bank’s digital and AI roadmap in a measurable way, or whether it primarily funds conventional balance-sheet growth in a lending market that remains highly competitive across the Gulf.

title: Fed names new payments chief
snippet: Federal Reserve Financial Services tapped Kim Robbins to succeed Mark Gould starting in November.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve’s financial services division has appointed Kim Robbins as its new top payments executive, tapping her to replace the retiring Mark Gould.

Federal Reserve Financial Services announced the appointment Thursday, picking a nearly 20-year Federal Reserve veteran to lead the division that provides payments services to financial institutions. She’ll step into the role on Nov. 16, according to the press release stating her appointment.

She has served as first vice president and chief operating officer at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City since March 2024 and has been with that reserve bank in some capacity since January 2012, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to heading to that regional bank, she worked for Federal Reserve Financial Services as the chief of enterprise services.

In a post last week on that social media site, Robbins said she was pleased to “return ‘home’ to payments.” She also gave a nod to the work that lies ahead.

“With rapid innovation transforming the industry, it is clear to me that we are in a pivotal moment in payments,” she said. “I look forward to partnering across the Federal Reserve System and with our industry stakeholders to advance modern, secure, and resilient payment services that meet the dynamic and evolving needs of financial institutions, businesses, and the American public.”

Gould is retiring after spending the last three years with a key focus on rolling out the Fed’s instant payments system FedNow, starting in mid 2023, and trying to lure banks across the country to join the system. As of this month, the central bank has attracted just over 1,900 U.S. banks and credit unions to use the real-time payments system.

With some 8,500 financial institutions in the U.S. eligible to use the system, the Fed has a ways to go in drawing more banks and credit unions to the new service. Last month, the Fed began offering a discount program to entice financial institutions to participate in the service.

Only U.S. financial institutions can join the system, which enables them to send payments in a matter of seconds or minutes, as opposed to transactions sometimes taking days to settle. The Fed launched the instant payments system in July 2023 in the hopes of bringing smaller banks into the realm of faster payments. That followed the start of a private real-time system, the RTP Network, by bigger banks that own The Clearing House in November 2017.

In late 2024, the Fed disclosed that it cost about $246 million to operate the FedNow payments system that year, after requiring about $100 million for development in 2023, according to a report from the central bank. 

The central bank this year has also been exploring how to extend the reach of the system across international borders. Last month, the Fed said the real-time system was “on the verge” of providing cross-border transaction “support,” but then it stopped short of saying how and when. 

Robbins has leadership experience both with respect to FedNow as well as the broader Federal Reserve Financial Services, the release said. 

Specifically, the release noted that she was FedNow’s chief administrative officer, leading the “functions supporting the program’s rapid scale-up across multiple Federal Reserve Banks,” plus “strengthening the governance, risk, compliance and legal structures” for the system.

Aside from FedNow, Robbins will oversee the Fed’s retail, wholesale and securities services for financial institutions, the release noted.

Before Robbins joined the Fed, she had an early start to her career in a different kind of retail sector. She worked for seven years for the GAP and Payless ShoeSource, managing various aspects of the retail chains’ business lines.

Between February 2017 and June 2019, Bedi and Mavanga operated a fraudulent investment scheme, cold-calling consumers and persuading them to invest in fake cryptoasset opportunities through companies including CCX Capital and Astaria Group LLP. At least 65 investors were defrauded and lost £1,541,799.

The FCA has identified and contacted victims of the fraud and will ensure that funds recovered through the confiscation process are returned to victims.

In July 2025, following an FCA prosecution, Raymondip Bedi was sentenced to 5 years and 4 months' imprisonment and Patrick Mavanga was sentenced to 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment for their roles in the scheme.

Steve Smart, joint executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Bedi and Mavanga defrauded investors and left them out of pocket. These orders bring victims a step closer to getting money back.

'We’ll keep coming after fraudsters and holding them to account.'

Notes to editors

Raymondip Bedi’s date of birth is 9 October 1989.

Patrick Mavanga’s date of birth is 24 November 1984.

FCA secures convictions against two individuals for £1.5m fraud.

Two individuals sentenced to a combined 12 years for £1.5m crypto fraud.

Confiscation orders are made under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and require offenders to repay the benefit they gained from criminal conduct or the value of their available assets, whichever is lower.

If the defendants fail to pay the confiscation orders within 3 months, Bedi will face up to an additional 5 years in prison and Mavanga could face up to 2 years.

The FCA has previously sought to contact affected investors. Anyone who believes they may have been affected and has not heard from the FCA should contact the FCA's Consumer Helpline.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5 year strategy.

The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more information about the FCA.

title: Three Things Every First Time Fund Manager Needs Before Raising Capital
snippet: Build an investment platform around investor trust and clear business goals—not appearances. Prioritize investor conversations, practical systems, and an aligned team. Expect setbacks, stay resilient, and remember that launching a fund is the start of a long-term commitment to investors. The post Three Things Every First Time Fund Manager Needs Before Raising Capital appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
If you’re thinking about launching an institutional investment platform, the legal side is only part of the story. The bigger challenge is building a business that can earn investor trust, manage complexity, and withstand the realities of fundraising and long-term execution.

In this conversation, Gary Anderson, a partner in Seward and Kissel’s mergers and acquisitions group, shares practical advice on what it takes to launch and grow an institutional-quality fund business: start with business goals, build around client needs, and expect surprises.

Start with the business—not the legal documents

Founders can assume that legal support is mainly about documents, compliance, and fixing issues after the fact. Gary’s point is that the best advice starts earlier, with a basic question: What business are you trying to build?

“All advice needs to be downstream from [the business goals].”

Legal decisions should support the strategy, not become the strategy. Gary compares legal issues to rocks and boulders in a stream: they matter, but the business goal is the flow. A technically sound structure is not enough if the business behind it is commercially weak. For fund managers, that means treating a launch as a business-design exercise. You’re building a platform that needs to attract capital, operate reliably, and adapt over time—not simply creating a vehicle.

Practical takeaway: Before getting lost in structure, define the outcome you want to create. Let that goal guide the decisions that follow.

“Institutional” means operational readiness—not bureaucracy

Being institutional isn’t about using the right label in a pitch deck. It means having an operating model that matches serious investors’ expectations. Gary describes institutionalization as a calibrated exercise in risk management and systems development. That may include:

Clear financial controls

Processes that can scale with the business

Risk management that accounts for less obvious issues

Incentives aligned with client outcomes

Systems that support good decision-making

But institutional doesn’t mean bureaucratic. Useful systems help manage the business; unnecessary layers can slow it down without giving investors meaningful confidence. The question isn’t, “Do we look institutional?” It’s, “Do our operations actually support institutional expectations?”

The traits that help founders build institutional platforms

Founders arrive with different backgrounds. People who have worked in institutional environments may already understand controls, risk management, and the complexity that comes with scale. But institutional thinking can also come from outside traditional asset management. 

The traits that matter include: Experience with controls and redundancy A strong idea is only one part of a fund business. Founders also need to understand how controls work, why redundancy matters, and how hidden risks can affect an organization. Comfort with complexity As a business grows, its moving parts interact. A small issue in one area can have consequences elsewhere. 

Experience managing complexity can help founders prepare for that reality. Empathy for clients Founders need to understand what clients require to feel confident—including compliance, transparency, and the assurance that their assets are being handled responsibly. Judgment about process The aim is to build systems that fit the business, not systems that exist simply to make it look mature. 

For emerging managers, that distinction can help avoid spending time and money on performative complexity. It’s useful for founders to assess their strengths and gaps honestly. If you know how to identify opportunities but need help building operational infrastructure, that’s valuable information to act on—not something to conceal.

Resilience is essential in fund formation

Launching a fund or investment platform is rarely a linear process. Some external factors can be anticipated, but few can be controlled. Even with a solid strategy and legal setup, founders should expect curveballs, disappointments, and slower-than-expected progress. Gary’s advice to first-time founders is straightforward: expect difficulty. Unrealistic expectations can lead to poor decisions. If you assume the process should move cleanly from launch to fundraising to scale, every obstacle can feel like evidence that something has gone wrong. In reality, obstacles are part of the work. Resilience in practice can mean:

Accepting that the path may not be linear

Leaving room for unexpected issues

Focusing on problem-solving rather than panic

Measuring progress over time

Staying focused on investor outcomes

Raising capital is not the finish line. It’s a promise to investors, and the years after launch are about delivering on it. That mindset turns launch from the ultimate goal into the beginning of an ongoing responsibility.

Three priorities for fund managers

1. Put resources toward the highest-return activities Gary notes that hiring a lawyer is rarely the highest-return use of a founder’s money right at the beginning. That doesn’t make legal advice unimportant. It means founders should be thoughtful about where their early resources go. During capital formation, direct conversations with potential investors can be especially valuable. Founders need to explain what they’re doing, why the strategy matters, why the opportunity is compelling, and why they’re the right people to execute it. The broader idea: validate the opportunity with the market, then refine the platform.

2. Surround the business with aligned people This includes advisors and the internal team. Gary emphasizes the value of a shared investor-first mentality. A small, aligned team can be more valuable than a larger group with unclear priorities. When choosing people to support the business, consider not only whether they can help, but whether they share the outcomes you’re working toward.

3. Expect surprises and stay focused on solutions Setbacks and uncertainty are part of building an institutional platform. The goal isn’t to eliminate all surprises; it’s to build the capacity to respond to them. Founders who stay focused on solving problems are better equipped to move through launch, growth, and the challenges that follow.

Think beyond launch day

Fund formation is not a finish line. It’s the beginning of a relationship with investors that needs to be maintained over time. The work continues after launch. Managers who build durable businesses understand that they are creating more than a single product: they are building an enterprise that may grow into a broader platform or support future funds. The goal isn’t simply to work harder or look institutional. It’s to build a business that can absorb difficulty without losing sight of its purpose. That’s how a platform moves from appearing institutional to operating that way.

Frequently asked questions

What does it mean to launch an institutional investment platform?

It means building an investment business with the systems, controls, risk management, and team alignment institutional investors expect. It’s about operational discipline and long-term reliability—not just a polished pitch. 

Why is resilience important for fund founders?

Fund formation is rarely a straight path. Investor conversations, operational challenges, timing, and external variables can all affect progress. Resilience helps founders stay focused when the process gets difficult. 

Is legal structure the most important part of launching a fund?

Legal structure matters, but it should support the business strategy rather than drive it. A strong platform starts with a clear business goal and builds its legal and operational framework around that goal. 

What do investors look for in an institutional manager?

Investors want confidence in the manager’s operating model, controls, alignment, and ability to handle complexity responsibly and protect investor capital. 

Should first-time founders build infrastructure first?

Not necessarily. Founders should prioritize the highest-return uses of their resources. Early on, that may mean validating the opportunity and having direct investor conversations before investing heavily in structure and process.

title: Tap Global Appoints Moorwand to Issue New Multi-Currency Mastercard
snippet: Tap Global's 400,000-user platform will offer customers direct multi-currency spending from app balances, with card interchange and FX as operating revenue. The post Tap Global Appoints Moorwand to Issue New Multi-Currency Mastercard appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Tap Global Group plc (AIM: TAP), the AIM-listed digital finance platform, has appointed Moorwand Ltd as issuer and Bank Identification Number sponsor for a new Tap Mastercard programme, extending an existing partnership that already underpins the e-money accounts in the Tap app.

The move is primarily a product upgrade. The current Tap card is euro-denominated, meaning that purchases in other currencies trigger a conversion at the point of sale. The new card is designed to let customers spend directly from whichever currency balances they hold in the app: a customer paid in sterling spends in sterling; a customer travelling in a local-currency market draws down a balance held in that currency. Tap says the multi-currency card has been its most-requested feature from its base of approximately 400,000 users.

The commercial logic

Arsen Torosian, CEO and co-founder at TAP Global PLC

The arrangement carries a direct revenue rationale. Card interchange fees and foreign-exchange margin are both operating revenue lines for the Group, alongside trading fees and what Tap calls Tap Earn income. Putting more currencies on a single card and expanding into additional markets widens the pool of transactions against which both revenue streams accrue. Tap did not disclose projected interchange volumes, FX spread assumptions or a timeline for the additional market launches.

Moorwand is an FCA-authorised Electronic Money Institution and a principal member of Mastercard, which means it can act as BIN sponsor without routing through a third-party processor for scheme access. That principal membership is commercially significant: it reduces the number of intermediaries between Tap and the Mastercard network, lowers per-transaction cost in principle and, according to Tap, gives the Group a single platform on which to develop new card features and payment use cases as it enters new markets.

Arsen Torosian, group CEO and co-Founder, said: “A multi-currency card has been the feature requested most often by our customers, and this programme delivers it. It also gives us a stronger foundation for new payment features and expansion into additional markets over time. Card interchange and FX are operating revenue, so every card we put in a customer’s hand earns for the Group.”

Market and regulatory context

The multi-currency prepaid card space is well-populated. Wise, Revolut and several other FCA-regulated e-money institutions already offer cardholders the ability to hold and spend in multiple currencies from a single account, and competition on FX spread is intense in that segment. For Tap, the differentiation proposition is integration with its crypto-adjacent digital finance app rather than a standalone prepaid product.

From a regulatory standpoint, card issuance in additional markets will require compliance with local licensing and Mastercard scheme rules on a market-by-market basis, as Tap acknowledges in its announcement. The FCA authorisation that Moorwand holds is valid in the UK and, under the post-Brexit framework, does not automatically passport into EU jurisdictions. Any European expansion will require its own regulatory pathway, either through Moorwand’s EU entity or a separate issuing arrangement. That incremental compliance overhead is worth watching as the Group’s market expansion plans become more specific.

The October 2025 e-money partnership with Moorwand provides a working foundation. Consolidating both the account and card infrastructure under a single principal partner reduces operational complexity and, in theory, should accelerate future product iteration. The near-term markers for investors and observers will be the timing of card launch for existing users, the specific additional markets targeted and any disclosure of early card-spend data.

The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.

We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.

The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'

Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.

'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'

In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation. 

Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

title: Amex dinged by Fed, OCC
snippet: American Express must pay a $350 million penalty after regulators cited “significant deficiencies” in its anti-money laundering program.
fullText:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Board concurrently issued enforcement actions against American Express and its subsidiaries Thursday over failures in their anti-money laundering programs.

American Express National Bank was hit with a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty by the OCC, while American Express and its travel-related services arm received a cease-and-desist from the Fed.

Amex’s bank subsidiary, based in Sandy, Utah, failed to tailor its Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering risk assessment to its business activities, according to the OCC, by focusing too much on its “relatively narrow” demand deposit account products and services and not enough on the risks in its “more dominant” credit and charge card products.

Additionally, the bank experienced “systemic breakdowns” in its suspicious activity monitoring and reporting processes, resulting in roughly $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity between June 2014 and May 2025, the OCC said.

The Fed called $308 billion-asset Amex’s AML program issues “enterprise wide,” but particularly an issue at its national bank subsidiary.

“The OCC expects banks of American Express’s size and complexity to devote sufficient resources to ensure compliance with laws and regulations designed to detect and prevent money laundering, which are critical to both economic and national security,” said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould in a prepared statement.

Amex’s banking subsidiary is now required to create an action plan within 90 days to address its compliance deficiencies as well as develop an effective BSA/AML risk assessment process and consumer due diligence and risk identification program, according the OCC order, It must also engage a third-party to conduct a suspicious activity review look-back.

Under the Fed order,, Amex is required to submit a plan to improve its enterprise-wide BSA/AML compliance risk management program. TRS must submit to the Fed a plan to address Office of Foreign Assets Control compliance.

Amex “takes its responsibility to combat financial crimes seriously,” and that it will address the concerns of both the Fed and the OCC, the company’s CEO, Stephen Squeri, said Thursday in a post on the Amex website.

“Over the last few years, we have engaged closely with regulators as we have strengthened our controls and with law enforcement to provide information,” Squeri said in the statement.

“While we have made meaningful progress, we know there is more work to do,” he said.

A portion of the civil money penalty was “reserved for in prior periods,” he said, and it does not impact the full-year 2026 guidance. The consent orders are not anticipated to affect Amex’s 2027 guidance, he said.

This is the first civil money penalty imposed on a bank by the OCC since the $450 million penalty it levied against TD in October 2024, according to OCC data.

Toronto-based TD’s penalty was also related to BSA/AML issues, but amounted to much more: more than $3.5 billion in penalties overall, and a $434 billion asset cap on TD’s U.S. retail banking operations.
