fullText:
Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026.

  

Speaker: Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges 

Event: Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026

Delivered: 5 October 2026  

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 9 minutes

Highlights:

The FCA’s wide-ranging reforms over recent years are making UK capital markets more effective, competitive and attractive.

Trust, market integrity and high standards set the foundations for sustainable growth, and it is crucial that we also enable informed risk-taking.

We’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets by supporting innovation, including tokenisation.

    

            						

The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth. 

I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.

The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years. 

We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.

This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.

We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.

In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme. 

And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.

The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.

Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.

We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.

These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.

Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

          

            						

Reforming from a position of strength

First, we are reforming from a position of strength, by building on the UK’s advantages.

The UK is home to deep, trusted and internationally connected capital markets. 

London continues to rank among the world’s leading financial centres. Our markets are respected and characterised by strong institutions and a reputation for integrity.

And the UK offers a full range of markets and services, supported by a diverse system of issuers, investors, intermediaries and infrastructure.

So our work programme is broad too. Covering primary markets, secondary markets, post-trade arrangements and a broad range of assets.

But successful markets cannot stand still.

Capital is increasingly mobile. Technology is reshaping markets. Private markets have grown. And new forms of trading and market infrastructure are emerging.

So our challenge is to preserve these strengths, whilst keeping UK markets dynamic and internationally competitive.

          

            						

Rebalancing risk

In some areas this requires us to think differently about regulation.

For a while, financial regulation became more detailed and prescriptive. Often for understandable reasons following periods of market stress.

But we know that growth, innovation and investment all depend on taking risk.

That is why our approach is founded on the principle of maintaining high standards while creating more space for informed risk-taking and innovation. 

This is especially relevant in wholesale markets, where professional participants assess opportunities and weigh risks every day.

Our role is to create regulation that enables this through clear rules and good disclosures, so that firms and investors can make informed decisions.

This is what we mean when we talk about rebalancing risk.

It does not mean lowering standards or weakening market integrity.

It means being deliberate about where regulation is needed and where market participants can take decisions themselves, armed with good information and appropriate disclosures.

In many cases, that means we can shift away from detailed prescription towards outcomes, transparency and accountability.

In doing so, we must never forget the underlying objective.

Ultimately, we want companies to have good options for how to raise capital, so they can invest and grow. And investors to have access to a broad range of investment opportunities.

Regulation cannot, on its own, drive economic growth. But good regulation and markets that work well are vital for a healthy economy.

          

            						

Turning reform into results

You can see our approach in the reforms we have already delivered.

We have completed around 30 capital-markets focused workstreams. And there’s an even larger number across the FCA’s broader work.

That’s too many to discuss individually in this speech. There’s a list below, but to summarise some of them:

In primary markets, we introduced once-in-a-generation changes to the UK listing regime, significantly reducing costs for issuers and supporting competitiveness with other jurisdictions. Since then, we have seen many corporate transactions that have been simplified as a result. And around 25 companies have joined the Main Market, including 7 IPOs in H1 2026.

Our new public offers framework raised the thresholds for when prospectuses are needed by companies raising capital and we also introduced public offer platforms to facilitate off-market fundraising. We have already seen a rise in capital raised by companies, including via debt markets, alongside the broader benefits of a simpler and more flexible regime.

In secondary markets, we have significantly improved transparency in bond and derivatives markets. This includes the bond consolidated tape, which launched in June – the first consolidated tape outside North America – which already has 1.6 million licences subscribed to it. These changes are shining a new light on UK markets, delivering a 70% increase in corporate bond trades and 30% for government bond trades observed in real time and enhancing the way market participants view the market.

We are moving towards an equity consolidated tape too and will appoint a provider next year. In the meantime, we launched a market activity report, so investors see the true scale of UK equity trading.

We have also responded to the growth of private markets through the creation of PISCES, a new market for trading in private company shares. Four operators have been authorised and we’ve seen seven transactions – involving companies ranging from tech firms, to brewers and board-game makers.

In post-trade, we’ve adjusted transaction reporting, with initial proposals estimated to save firms £100m per year.

And we’ve altered some of the clearing and margining rules, including increasing the clearing threshold for commodity derivatives following volatility in commodity markets.

On the investor side, we are streamlining regulatory requirements for the asset management sector, via the AIFMD review, and supporting the government in its review of the pension market.

We’re also supporting retail participation by improving access to investment advice and simplifying product information.

And our changes to primary market rules have positively impacted retail investment. We’ve seen a 50% increase in the value of retail-denominated corporate bonds and an increase in domestic retail investor allocation in fundraisings.

We are not done though.

A range of further reforms are planned or underway.

For example, on securitisation markets; listed company disclosures; benchmarks; and rules on clearing and margining.

We’re always in listening mode. So if you have ideas that would benefit UK markets please tell us.

          

            						

Competitiveness without compromise

We are doing this work to make markets work better, which is our statutory objective.

By doing that, we support growth and international competitiveness.

Capital is mobile. Businesses have choices about where they raise finance, invest and operate. The UK cannot ignore that reality.

But competitiveness does not come from a race to the bottom.

The UK's reputation for openness, stability and high standards is a strategic asset.

Our approach is pragmatic. We will challenge inherited rules when they no longer serve markets effectively, learn from other jurisdictions, and recognise the value of international consistency.

But we will do so without compromising market integrity, which provides the bedrock for sustainable growth.

          

            						

Preparing for tomorrow’s markets

I want to finish by talking about how we’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets.

We want to support innovation. To ensure markets evolve and use technology that opens up opportunities, efficiencies and encourages new entrants.

One example is working with firms to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI. Through our AI Lab, the AI Consortium with the Bank, and innovation sandboxes that allow firms to test ideas with us. 

And we are enabling firms and markets to explore tokenisation.

With the Bank and Treasury, we set up the Digital Securities Sandbox, which will support issuance of the new digital gilt (or DIGIT) early next year. Many think that the success of DIGIT can catalyse digital activity in UK.

We have worked with industry on new rules and governance for tokenised investment funds and the launch of the UK’s first fully-native tokenised fund.

And with Treasury and the Bank we’ve developed a regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But we are at a critical point. Keeping pace with other jurisdictions will require effective coordination between the private and public sectors. Industry leadership will be at least as important as public policy. 

Firms need to build, scale and innovate, moving beyond pilots to demonstrate real commercial use.

The UK’s Wholesale Digital Markets Champion, Chris Woolard, is playing a key role in coordinating the sector.

We know that regulatory clarity matters too. That’s why in May we published a joint vision with the Bank of England, setting out the regulatory principles for tokenised wholesale markets.

The feedback was clear. Industry wants to move quickly. In turn, we will provide certainty in areas such as prudential treatment, custody and market infrastructure.

We share the sense of urgency.

In coming weeks we will publish a joint roadmap, setting out how the UK’s wholesale markets will adapt as we work collectively to realise the benefits from tokenisation and digitalization.

Our objective is not to predict exactly what future markets will look like.

It is to ensure that our regulatory framework can adapt as markets evolve.

          

            						

Conclusion

We want UK capital markets to remain among the most trusted in the world, whilst also being among the most innovative, competitive and attractive. Markets that allow businesses to raise capital, help investors, and support the wider economy.

Our wide-ranging reforms have already delivered positive outcomes, across a variety of markets.

The approach is to build on the UK’s strengths and enable informed risk-taking, while preserving the trust, integrity and high standards on which successful markets depend.

The programme of reform will continue to evolve as markets change.

But the direction is clear. We are building markets that are ready not only for today's economy but for tomorrow's as well.

title: Where platforms are losing (and winning) merchants: Inside switching triggers
snippet: Merchants are willing to switch. Learn which platform factors drive loyalty and retention.
fullText:
Software providers have less room than ever to assume merchants will stay put.

For the second year in a row, more than 60% of merchants say they have an appetite for switching platforms. In 2025, that figure stood at 62%, up from 55% in 2023, according to the 2026 Merchant Insider Report, which surveyed more than 1,500 businesses across Australia, the UK and the US.

Software providers need to understand what causes businesses to reconsider their current platform and what gives them a reason to stay. 

Payment satisfaction is the #1 reason businesses are unlikely to switch software providers. 

For platforms, payments are a key indicator of whether merchants feel supported enough to stay or frustrated enough to look elsewhere. 

Where platforms lose: when “good enough” stops being enough

Switching triggers point to stagnation, friction and poor fit more than any single product gap.

Among businesses likely to switch, the report found:

32% cite newer, more innovative software options

28% say they spend too much time managing their current solution

28% want a provider better suited to their industry

27% say integrations no longer meet requirements

25% say their contract is ending

The report also found that 25% of likely switchers mention bad customer experiences using payment capabilities.

Together, these findings show how operational frustrations become switching triggers. When software takes too much time to manage, integrations fall short and payment experiences frustrate customers, the platform may no longer fit the business. 

That is where platforms begin to lose ground. Not because one feature is missing, but because the overall experience feels harder than it should.

Where platforms win: when payments strengthen loyalty

When the payment experience is reliable, easy to manage and well-integrated, it reinforces the value of the platform around it. Payments support the way merchants work. 

The platforms winning merchants are making payment capabilities feel current, useful and native to everyday workflows. That does not require chasing every headline-grabbing feature. It requires practical capabilities that help merchants accept the payment types they need, connect reliably to other systems, move money efficiently and keep pace with customer expectations.

Flexibility is becoming part of the retention equation

Another pattern emerges across the switching triggers: merchants are looking for platforms that adapt to their business, not the other way around.

Some merchants need simple payment capabilities, while others need more complex workflows, stronger integration support or additional ways to manage money movement. Those needs can shift as they grow. 

For software providers, the right payments relationship can make that flexibility easier to deliver. When payment capabilities can expand alongside merchant needs, platforms have more room to retain customers through different stages of growth.

Regional triggers show different routes to the same risk

The report revealed regional differences in platform priorities. 

In Australia, businesses are especially focused on innovation, time spent managing solutions and integration improvements. In the UK, industry fit, innovation and time spent managing the solution rise to the top. In the US, innovation, integration improvements and bad customer payment experiences stand out.

The priorities vary, but merchants are consistently measuring platforms by how well they fit their business. 

What switching triggers should tell software providers

Switching triggers are product map clues. 

If merchants are spending too much time managing their current solution, the opportunity may be to reduce manual work. If integrations no longer meet requirements, the opportunity may be to improve reliability. If innovation is driving switching consideration, the opportunity may be to make product improvements more visible. 

If customer payment experiences are disappointing, the opportunity is to make the payment journey easier and more trustworthy. 

The loyalty opportunity

Merchants are more willing to switch than they were a few years ago. But they are not unreachable. The same report that shows rising willingness to switch also shows the strongest reason they stay: satisfaction with payments.

That is the opportunity. Platforms that make payments feel reliable, flexible and valuable give merchants a clear reason to stay. Platforms that let payments become rigid, disconnected or outdated give them a reason to look elsewhere.

The switching signals are getting harder to ignore. For software providers, the path forward is not to assume merchants will stay put. It is to make staying feel like the smarter choice.

Get all the switch signals in the full report

2026 Merchant Insider Report breaks down the biggest switching triggers, shifting merchant expectations and the payment experiences driving long-term loyalty.

title: Block envisions bitcoin for all
snippet: The company’s head of bitcoin, Miles Suter, has two big tasks: Make bitcoin a routine payment tool and change the global financial system.
fullText:
Block executive Miles Suter envisions a day when bitcoin is functional, everyday digital money used as easily as cards and cash for routine transactions. 

To get there, Suter – the head of bitcoin and stablecoin at Block – has set out to make payments between millions of American consumers and Square merchants happen in bitcoins.

“We’re in a unique position as a large company with huge segments on both sides of the counter,” Suter said Wednesday, alluding to U.S. consumers and merchants in Square’s point of sale ecosystem. “I believe that there’s no company in the world doing more for bitcoin than Block.”

Suter joined Block nine years ago. The company’s first bitcoin service, bitcoin sales on Cash App, launched in January 2018, with about 24 million active users purchasing the digital currency since then.

But Block has much larger aspirations for bitcoin than merely selling it. Those ambitions are driven by the company’s top executive and long-time bitcoin booster Jack Dorsey.

Enabling bitcoin payments is key, Suter said in an interview. “Jack really believes in the mission of bitcoin as everyday money, and so those are the things I’m always thinking about as we roll out new products and how they can eventually lead to that endpoint.”

To increase awareness of bitcoin, Block launched its first consumer advertising campaign last week in a bid to push the digital currency into the consciousness of what it termed “60 million bitcoin curious Americans,” a figure the company derived from an August survey it commissioned.

The video clips in Block’s “Bitcoin Does” campaign spotlight affordability issues and consumers’ frustration with issues such as inflation, merchants’ transaction fees and rising housing costs. The campaign is mainly being shown on major social media sites, like Instagram, and on Fox Sports television. Ads will also show before two major Hollywood films slated for December releases.

Dorsey, Block’s billionaire founder, has been a bitcoin enthusiast for several years and has overseen expansion of the digital asset into several areas of the company’s business. “I don’t think there is anything more important in my lifetime to work on,” Dorsey said at a 2021 bitcoin conference, CNBC reported.

Block’s effort to promote bitcoin use among consumers comes a year after the company integrated bitcoin payments into the Square point-of-sale services in October 2025. Square also allows merchants to convert part of their card sales into bitcoin.

Another Block business, Cash App, has about 59 million active users of its digital wallet, while Square counts about 4 million sellers on its system. Block offers a 5% discount in bitcoin for Cash App users who pay with the digital currency at a Square merchant.

“I don’t think anybody else has an opportunity to kick off a two-sided marketplace like this,” Suter said of the Cash App-Square interaction. “People have talked about like, ‘Well, maybe bitcoin's relevant finally when you can use it to go buy your daily coffee.’ And now, that’s definitely a reality.”

Block sees consumers’ conversion from traditional fiat money to electronic bitcoin funds as a three-part journey: accessibility to the currency through Cash App; security in its digital wallet; and daily use through Cash App consumers and Square merchants.

“We believe bitcoin needs to be money,” to make it a long-term reality, Suter said. 

In terms of bitcoin’s digital cousin, stablecoins, he considers them “a meaningful step on the long-term road towards broad-based bitcoin adoption by the world,” Suter said. Stablecoins are less volatile than bitcoins due to their 1-to-1 backing with fiat currencies.

“It gets people comfortable with this concept of a digital currency,” he said. However, he added, stablecoins “are an extension and a technological innovation of that same” financial system that operates on fiat currencies. 

That contrasts with bitcoin, which is a decentralized digital asset that has no government or central bank control and is subject to extreme price swings. 

“For me, bitcoin is a more revolutionary, upgraded system,” Suter said. “They’re not necessarily in the same ballpark.”

Stablecoin-payment efforts to date “don’t necessarily have the right posture,” he said, because a digital wallet and POS system may not locate each other or offer the proper incentives for people to try the new payment method.

“We believe in the principles of Bitcoin, and really one of the principles of bitcoin is having a really long-term time horizon, and that’s no shade to stablecoins,” Suter said. “They’re a very useful tool, especially in developing markets. And in the long run, they will assist bitcoin on its path to being everyday money.”

Block’s ecosystem of bitcoin products includes direct sales to customers and transaction revenue through Cash App; a $250 digital bitcoin wallet it launched in April; and a business unit that sells hardware and software tools for bitcoin mining. Direct sales account for the bulk of bitcoin revenues, according to Block’s annual report.

In the second quarter, Block’s gross profit from bitcoin fell 31%, to $72 million, from the same period last year due to Block’s “strategic decision” to trim fees for bitcoin purchases. It also removed fees from purchases over $2,000, and acknowledged that “bitcoin trading dynamics” in the quarter contributed to the profit decline. Block’s bitcoin revenue dipped 13% to $1.89 billion in the second quarter.

Beyond consumers’ comfort and adoption of bitcoin, merchants’ desires for a lower-cost payment rail may ultimately push wider use of the digital coins, Suter said.

“The Square side is still a bit more nascent, but when we do talk to merchants, the thing that they do key in on are those cost savings, and that is what we’ve led with in a lot of our messaging to existing and prospective merchants,” he said, noting that the current card-based system is “really good in a lot of ways.” 

“Ultimately, I do think (costly network fees) will be one of the things that helps to kickstart this, but changing the global financial system is probably the hardest thing I could imagine,” Suter said. “And so I just zoom out again, sometimes, and know that this is a really long-term journey and mission that I’m committed to and Block is committed to.”

We asked the Court to make Arthur Temlett, trading as Abacus Insurance Consultants ('Abacus'), bankrupt. This is known as sequestration in Scotland. The Sheriff granted our application on 27 August 2026.

  

            						

Emma Porter of Aver Chartered Accountants ('Aver') was appointed as trustee. She will now assess Mr Temlett’s financial affairs and seek to distribute any recovered funds to creditors.

Arthur Temlett is awaiting trial on embezzlement charges brought following an investigation by Police Scotland.

On 21 January 2025, we took action to protect consumers by stopping Arthur Temlett from carrying out any regulated activities, including acting as an insurance broker. This was because of concerns that he may have sold home and motor insurance without passing premium payments on to the insurance provider.

          

            						

  

Who to contact if you’re a customer

Customers of Abacus can contact the trustee, at Aver on:

Telephone: 0330 555 6155

Email: [email protected]

Address: PO Box 24213, Edinburgh EH1 9AT 

          

        

Information for customers 

    

      

      						I purchased home or car insurance from Abacus, what should I do?
			
    

    

						

As Abacus stopped regulated activities in January 2025, we expect that most previous policies will have expired or been renewed with another provider by now. However, if customers are concerned, they should contact their insurance providers directly to check that their insurance is valid and in place. If they are uninsured, they should arrange alternative cover immediately.

Alternative insurance can be bought directly from an insurance firm or arranged via an insurance broker. The British Insurance Brokers’ Association offers a service for customers who need help finding an authorised broker.

Anyone who believes they have paid for a policy that does not exist should report this to Police Scotland in the first instance by dialling 101 and using the crime reference number: CR/0470100/24.

Customers should also contact the trustee, using the contact details above. The trustee will explain to you what to do if you are affected.

			

  

      

      						I have an existing complaint at Abacus, what happens now?
			
    

    

						

If you’ve made a complaint against Abacus, you may have a claim if you are due any money in compensation.

You should contact the trustee for more details on how complaints or claims will be dealt with, using the contact details above.

			

  

      

      						What is the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS)?
			
    

    

						

The Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protects consumers when UK financial services firms go out of business.

Whether you’re covered by the FSCS will depend on:

The firm.

Type of activity the firm does.

The FSCS is operationally independent of the FCA. The FSCS decides whether compensation is payable under our compensation rules.

			

  

      

      						Do I need to use a claims management company or a law firm?
			
    

    

						

For the vast majority of consumers, there is no benefit in involving a third party in reclaiming your assets.

If you use a claims management company (CMC) or law firm to assist in the return of your assets, they will likely seek a fee which may reduce what you get back.

If you are considering using a CMC or law firm to assist with the return of your assets, we suggest you first discuss this with the trustee using the contact details provided above. 

			

  

  

            						

Protecting yourself from scams

Fraudsters sometimes claim to be from legitimate firms authorised by us, or (in the case of bankruptcy) the appointed trustee.

Be wary of fraudsters pretending to be Abacus, Arthur Temlett or the trustee and asking you to pay money to get your money back.

If you get an unexpected call from someone claiming to be Abacus, Arthur Temlett or the trustee you should:

End the call straight away.

Call them back using the phone numbers above.

Find out how to protect yourself from scams, including recovery room scams.

title: Visa-Mastercard payouts top $631M
snippet: The tally of merchants receiving funds from a $5.5 billion settlement with the networks is nearing 700,000, according to a claims update.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                

The tally of merchants receiving funds from a $5.5 billion settlement with the networks is nearing 700,000, according to a claims update.

        

            

        Published Oct. 12, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Merchants that accepted Visa and Mastercard payments may be eligible to claim part of a lawsuit settlement. A sticker on glass at the front of a business on February 11, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois.
            
        
            Scott Olson via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Merchants have received about $631.7 million to date as part of a multi-billion dollar class-action lawsuit settlement with the card networks Visa and Mastercard, according to a court filing Friday.

The damages disbursements have gone to 689,340 merchants so far, including $212.8 million from a second partial distribution that began last month, class administrator Epiq said in the filing with the U.S. District Court in Brooklyn, New York.

District Judge Brian Cogan approved the second distribution in June as part of his oversight of a $5.5 billion settlement with the two largest U.S. card networks. About 84,000 merchant claimants who sued as part of the class action are covered in the second round of merchant payouts.

The settlement partially resolved an antitrust case in which merchants alleged the two network giants charged them excessive interchange fees when customers paid with a credit or debit card. The merchants’ class includes any U.S. business that accepted Visa or Mastercard-branded cards between Jan. 1, 2004, and Jan. 25, 2019. 

The settlement fund held $5.02 billion as of Sept. 30, following the distributions to merchants, according to the report by Epiq, the class administrator in the litigation. The next quarterly report to the court on claims will be filed in January.

The settlement for the damages portion of the case was reached in 2018 and received final approval by a federal judge the following year, followed by appeals. 

About 1.47 million merchants filed claims in the case as of a February 2025 deadline. About 2.12 million merchant tax identification numbers were registered as part of the overall group of business owners due a potential payout from the settlement, according to the report.

Separately, U.S. Magistrate Judge Joseph Marutollo, who is assigned to help the court in the case, last week approved Epiq’s request for $21.4 million for its administration work from April through August. 

Cogan has scheduled a hearing next month on a second part of the case, a proposed settlement that covers injunctive relief in the swipe-fee litigation. 

It is supported by the card networks and attorneys for the class of plaintiffs, with the litigation dating to October 2005. Multiple large merchants, including Walmart, Circle K and DoorDash, oppose the settlement and have urged Cogan to reject it.

title: The Earnings Call Went 24/7. Wall Street’s Clock Didn’t
snippet: Bitget CEO Gracy Chen argues that tokenised stocks and always-on venues are moving price discovery into the hours when US exchanges are closed. The post The Earnings Call Went 24/7. Wall Street’s Clock Didn’t appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
US equity markets still work to a trading day that ends at 4pm in New York, and companies time their results around it. Tokenised versions of the same shares, and perpetual futures that track them, now trade around the clock on crypto exchanges, including overnight and at weekends when the primary exchanges are shut.

Gracy Chen, CEO of Bitget

Gracy Chen is chief executive of Bitget, a cryptocurrency exchange that lists tokenised stocks and equity perpetuals. In this contributed piece she argues that price discovery is moving to venues that never close, and that traditional markets will have to respond. The views are her own.

There is a choreography to earnings season that everyone in finance knows by heart. A company reports after the closing bell. Analysts and reporters spend the evening pulling the numbers apart. The rest of us wait for the next morning, when the market opens, and the stock finally moves. That sequence has organised professional investing for decades, and it rests on one quiet assumption: that between the report and the open, nothing can really trade.

That assumption is no longer true, and I don’t think most of Wall Street has noticed.

The same household names, Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, now trade around the clock. Tokenised versions of them, and the derivatives that track them, can now change hands at 2am on a Sunday as well as at 2pm on a Tuesday. So when a company reports at 4.05pm, and its guidance disappoints, the repricing no longer waits politely for the next session. It starts immediately, somewhere in the world, on a venue that never closed.

I can put a number on it. Over the weekend of 13 July, big geopolitical news broke while US exchanges were dark. On our platform, trading in tokenised stocks ran more than ten times a normal week, led by tokenised Nvidia. Investors were repricing exposure to major American companies in real time, while the primary exchanges remained closed. That is a preview.

Here is why it matters, and it has nothing to do with crypto. Price discovery follows whoever is open when the news breaks. If a story lands at 8pm and the only markets awake are the always-on ones, that is where the first layer of discoverability begins. The 9.30am open stops being the main event and becomes a catch-up mechanism. A market that keeps bankers’ hours in a world of around-the-clock information is quietly giving away the one thing an exchange is for: setting the price.

And this shift could accelerate as AI agents become a more active part of trading. More than half of our users already lean on AI tools; an agent doesn’t keep office hours, and it doesn’t wait for New York to wake up. You cannot build autonomous, always-on trading on top of a market that closes at 4pm and all weekend. The software is ready but the market’s clock is the bottleneck.

None of this means the old frictions were pointless. Thin overnight liquidity is real, and so is the risk of violent moves when fewer people are around to take the other side. As an exchange operator, I see these trade-offs directly. But they are arguments for building the always-on market carefully, with deeper liquidity and real market-makers on the other side at 3am, not for pretending the clock still holds. Demand does not wait for permission but instead moves to wherever it can act.

Today, the tokenised versions of traditional assets are a rounding error, a fraction of a per cent of the markets they mirror. I think that will reach close to 10 per cent within five years. In dollar terms, that is trillions, not a niche: trillions of dollars of stocks, funds, and commodities that will trade whenever their owner, or their owner’s AI agent, decides to, instead of whenever an exchange decides to open its doors.

The earnings call already went 24/7. The information, the reaction, and increasingly the trading does too. The only open question is whether the market itself stays open to meet it. We’ve made our bet by building the one that doesn’t close. The rest of finance will have to decide how long it can afford to keep the lights off.

title: Treasury taps data to fend off fraud
snippet: The U.S. department has increased its scrutiny of payments using new sources of data in an attempt to stem past ‘pay and chase’ patterns.
fullText:
The Treasury Department is increasingly using data to help prevent the U.S. government from sending payments to bad actors, Secretary Scott Bessent said this week in an update on fighting fraud.

Newly deployed safeguards, including the ability to tap additional sources of data, helped protect some $3.7 trillion in payments, the department said in an Oct. 6 press release. 

“Treasury continues to transform how the federal government protects taxpayer dollars by using better data, stronger controls, and advanced technology to stop fraud and improper payments before money goes out the door,” Bessent said in the release.

The federal government’s increased vigilance in fighting fraud comes as artificial intelligence increases the threats posed not only to government agencies, but also consumers and companies. Indeed, some industry professionals have said that the federal government has not been playing a significant enough role in helping to combat the mushrooming fraud problem.

The threat of scams, where fraudsters induce consumers, companies or other organizations, to send payments under false pretenses has become a particularly troubling issue. Americans are bilked out of $119 billion annually, according to estimates in a March report from the Consumer Federation of America that included an approximation of incidents that go unreported. 

Treasury’s increased scrutiny of government payments followed an executive order last year from President Donald Trump’s calling for a crackdown on “fraud, waste and abuse” that might affect the government’s trillions of dollars in annual payments. Trump’s predecessor, then President Joe Biden, had also sought to thwart the rising fraud.

“Financial fraud threatens the integrity of Federal programs and undermines trust in Government. Agencies’ past underinvestment in technology and longstanding challenges with access to accurate data has prevented them from more fully safeguarding taxpayer dollars against fraud and improper payments,” the White House said in that March 2025 order. 

The Treasury department contended that its fraud-fighting capabilities had improved in fiscal year 2026, which ended on Sept. 30, over the prior year, by expanding access to data that helps identify fraudulent accounts. The government added nine data sets to better verify identities for payments and to improve screening of payments.

The federal government has sought to move away from past practices that amounted to ‘pay and chase,’ in which payers find themselves in the position of making improper payments and then striving, usually in vain, to recoup losses.

As of fiscal year 2026, most federal programs now have access to the additional data sources aimed at helping to identify fraudulent accounts, up from just 4% in the prior fiscal year. The remainder of programs are expected to have the access by early in the 2027 fiscal year, the release said.

As part of the improved screening, the government stopped 13,500 payments worth $175 million that were headed to falsified identities of people who were found to be deceased, the release said. 

In the White House order, the Government Accountability Office estimated the federal government’s losses at between $233 billion and $521 billion per year due to fraud.

snippet: The card network giant said it won approval from the Chinese government to begin preparing to offer card services domestically in the country.
fullText:

The card network giant said it won approval from the Chinese government to begin preparing to offer card services domestically in the country.

        

            

        Published Oct. 13, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The largest U.S. card network is chasing its smaller rival, Mastercard, in seeking to offer services domestically in China.
            
        
            The image by Sean MacEntee is licensed under CC BY 2.0
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Visa said Tuesday in a press release that it has won approval from the Chinese government for “an application to prepare” to begin clearing card transactions in the country.

The San Francisco-based card network, the largest in the U.S., said it will “continue its efforts to complete the process” so it can begin offering the services. 

“This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China’s domestic payments market,” the release said.

Dive Insight:

Visa CEO Ryan McInerney noted in the release that the card network had been a part of China’s payments landscape for some 40 years, given the use of its services by international card holders in the country.

“We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the [People’s Bank of China’s] regulations, to begin operating domestically in China,” McInerney said in the release.

Visa is chasing its smaller U.S. rival, Mastercard, which won approval to operate within China in 2023. Purchase, New York-based Mastercard and a Chinese counterpart formed a Beijing joint venture, called Mastercard NetsUnion Information Technology, began processing payments in 2024 for cards issued by the country’s banks, according to a press release at that time.

The U.S.-based card companies had sought since at least 2017 to gain entry to the domestic Chinese market, in the hopes of attracting banks and consumers in that populous country to their services. Having the wherewithal to sell services in the country domestically can supplement and complement the U.S. card companies’ existing cross-border services flowing through China.

Still, U.S. card companies face significant domestic competition in China. They’re up against the dominant government-backed China UnionPay, which likely has an edge in attracting Chinese banks as card issuers.

“We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” McInerney said in the release.

title: Finance leaders fight deepfakes
snippet: Corporate finance departments are grappling with AI-enabled fraud, according to the results of a new survey by Early Warning Services’ Certos.
fullText:
Encountering fraud that looks like the workings of an artificial intelligence tool? You’re not alone.

According to a new survey of 230 senior financial leaders conducted by Early Warning Services’ fraud prevention unit Certos, as many as 81% of respondents said their company had experienced an attempted fraud that involved, or appeared to involve, “AI-generated or AI-enhanced content or techniques” within the last year.

A similar share (79%) said they were very concerned that AI-enabled fraud could negatively affect trust in their organization.

The potential repercussions of AI-powered fraud, evidently, are sweeping. In response to an open-ended question about their biggest concerns about AI-enabled fraud or scams, just about one in five respondents (21%) cited the potential for executive deepfake impersonation. The most common response to that question, cited by 43% of respondents, was payment diversion, followed by detection gaps or control lags, named by 38% of respondents.

As one anonymous CFO of a Fortune 500 company put it: “Biggest concern is a convincing fake request slipping through and sending company money to the wrong place.Certos conducted the online survey Aug. 7-21 and received 79 responses from leaders at Fortune 500 companies, 127 from venture-backed companies and 24 from charitable organizations. The survey didn’t include responses from banks and credit unions, investment managers, financial services or fintech firms or those working on AI model development or AI services.

Detection gaps

Fraudsters who use AI may be likelier to slip through the cracks, too. Eighty-four percent of respondents said that AI-enabled fraud is much, or somewhat more difficult, to detect than traditional fraud. And, where most respondents (87%) believed they were very, or somewhat, prepared for the “sophistication of AI-enabled fraud and scams,” only half were confident they could identify such fraud or scam attempts “before money leaves the organization.”

Certos’ report comes at a time when businesses across many industries continue to loudly and enthusiastically embrace new AI tools in the name of productivity, even as purveyors of the technology themselves continue to issue dire warnings about the threats posed by their own products. In a leaked prospectus document obtained by Reuters, for instance, Anthropic officials explicitly said that advanced AI could lead to “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

In an email, a Certos spokesperson acknowledged that “AI can make fraud easier to create, scale and disguise.”

“But the bigger takeaway from the research is that this is becoming a commercial banking issue, not simply a cybersecurity issue,” the spokesperson said. “More broadly, we do not view these findings as a reason to retreat from technology. They show that the threat is evolving quickly and that financial institutions need to continue evolving their defenses along with it.”

Executives are certainly not the only ones facing AI-related fraud, with recent research by Consumer Reports showing that nine in 10 Americans have encountered at least one type of cyberattack or digital scam. “Scams are felt by everyone and rapidly evolving thanks to AI,” said Craig Newmark, founder of Craigslist and the “Take 9” cybersecurity public awareness campaign, in that report.

In a world of compounding fraud, driven by AI or otherwise, whose job is it to stop such incursions? The Certos report suggests that companies are increasingly leaning on their financial institutions for some help. Ninety-three percent of respondents said that AI-enabled fraud risk is changing how their organization thinks about its financial institution partners.

When asked to name their top three expectations of their financial institutions, more than half (51%) of respondents said they’re looking for “better detection of suspicious activity.” Early Warning Services is owned by some of the top banks in the U.S.

In a statement, Certos General Manager Ben Chance said that the solution to AI-enabled fraud rests on “having the inter-bank network intelligence to help determine whether the receiving account actually belongs to the person or business the sender thinks they’re paying before money leaves the bank.”

In an email, a Certos spokesperson pointed out that the survey shows “strong agreement that this problem cannot be solved by any one institution or sector alone.”

Response to fraud, the spokesperson said, has to “extend across the ecosystem.”

“Telecom providers, payment networks, marketplaces, law enforcement, regulators and policymakers all have roles to play,” the spokesperson said.

Early Warning Services officially launched Certos in April in an effort to solidify and rebrand the company’s fraud prevention efforts. “The industry is at this point where we really, as an industry, need to reinvest in our fraud tools and our fraud capabilities and keep up with the pace of innovation that we’re seeing from threat actors,” Chance said in an interview at that time.
